Background and Factual Matrix
1. Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018 are being considered together. In
Appeal No. 56 of 2018, Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution Corporation
Limited (“TANGEDCO”) challenges the order dated 19.09.2017 passed by
the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (“Central Commission”/
“Respondent No. 1”/ “CERC”) in Petition No. 235/TT/2016 concerning
transmission tariff for some assets forming part of the transmission scheme
associated with the Coastal Energen Private Limited and Ind-Barath Power
(Madras) Limited generation projects in the Tuticorin area.
2. In Appeal No. 329 of 2018, TANGEDCO has challenged the order
dated 21.11.2017 passed by CERC in Petition No. 71/TT/2017 whereby
CERC had determined tariff for some other assets forming part of the above
mentioned transmission scheme.
3. The Appellant, TANGEDCO is a distribution licensee in the State of
Tamil Nadu. Respondent No. 1 is CERC which passed the Impugned Orders.
Page 4 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
Respondent No. 2 is Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (“PGCIL”)
which implemented the transmission assets and filed the tariff petition before
the Central Commission. Respondent Nos. 3 to 16 and 19 comprise
transmission utilities, distribution companies and electricity departments in
the Southern Region. Respondent Nos. 17 and 18 are Coastal Andhra
Private Limited (“Coastal Energen”) and Ind-Barath Power (Madras) Limited
(“Ind-Barath”), respectively. Respondent No. 20 is Central Transmission
Utility of India Limited (“CTUIL”).
4. The common transmission system was discussed at the 29th and 30th
meetings of the Standing Committee on Power System Planning held on
27.08.2009 and 13.04.2010. The title of the approved scheme indicates that
scheme was primarily meant for evacuation of generation from generating
stations owned by Coastal Energen and Ind-Barath. It comprised pooling
stations at Tuticorin and Salem; the LILO of both circuits of the Tuticorin JV-
Madurai 400 kV double-circuit line at Tuticorin; the Salem Pooling Station-
Salem 400 kV double-circuit line; the Tuticorin-Salem 765 kV double-circuit
and Salem-Madhugiri 765 kV single-circuit lines, both initially to be charged
at 400 kV; and associated bays. Each generating company was to develop
dedicated line from its switchyard to Tuticorin Pooling Station.
5. PGCIL, which at that point of time was also entrusted the role of CTU,
granted long-term access (“LTA”) of 1,100 MW to Coastal Energen against
its proposed 1,200 MW project and 900 MW to Ind-Barath against its
proposed 1,320 MW project. Of the aggregate 2,000 MW LTA, 1,045 MW
was indicated to remain in the Southern Region, while 550 MW and 405 MW
was indicated to flow to the Western Region and Northern Region
respectively.
Page 5 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
6. TANGEDCO has pointed out that at a special meeting of the Southern
Regional Power Committee on 25.11.2010, concerns were raised about
transmission charges attributable to independent power producers whose
beneficiaries had not been identified. PGCIL stated that the generators would
bear the charges until firm beneficiaries were identified. TANGEDCO
subsequently entered into a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) for 558 MW
with Coastal Energen.
7. The investment approval for the scheme was granted by PGCIL’s
board of directors on 19.09.2011 while revised cost estimates were approved
in 2017. TANGEDCO submitted that the project of Ind-Barath got abandoned
and Coastal Energen’s dedicated evacuation line was not built until
29.07.2016; and beneficiaries for the balance capacity, other than 558 MW
to Tamil Nadu, had not been firmed up.
8. By the Impugned Orders dated 19.09.2017 and 21.11.2017 in
Petition Nos. 235/TT/2016 and 71/TT/2017, respectively, the Central
Commission approved the commercial operation dates of the
respective transmission assets as 13.11.2016 and 23.10.2016, and
held that the associated transmission charges would be recovered
through the Point of Connection (PoC) mechanism. Aggrieved thereby,
TANGEDCO filed the present appeals.
9. The Appellant in Appeal No. 56 of 2018 has prayed for the following
relief before us:
“1. to set aside the order dated 19.09.17 passed by the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission in petition No. 235/TT/2016; and
2. pass any other order or orders as this Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal
may deem fit and proper in the facts of the case.”
Page 6 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
10. The Appellant in Appeal No. 329 of 2018 has prayed for the following
relief before us:
“1. to set aside the order dated 22/11/2017 passed by the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission in 71/TT/2017; and
2. pass any other order or orders as this Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal
may deem fit and proper in the facts of the case.”
11. The common factual matrix is that the system was planned against
aggregate LTA of 2,000 MW of Coastal Energen and Ind-Barath.
TANGEDCO had a PPA for 558 MW with Coastal Energen while the balance
capacity/ beneficiaries had not been firmed up. CERC’s Impugned orders in
Petition Nos. 235/TT/2016 and 71/TT/2017 held that the respective
assets were in use as part of the meshed network and directed recovery of
their charges through the PoC mechanism.
Issues for Consideration
12. TANGEDCO in both the Appeals had raised several issues, however
during the course of the hearing they pressed only the issues related to
declaration of commercial operation and sharing of transmission charges.
Accordingly, we have formulated the following issues for our consideration:
Issue 1: Whether the respective assets validly achieved COD
under the 2014 Tariff Regulations?
Issue 2: Whether the subject transmission assets could be
included in the PoC mechanism and their charges recovered
from DICs, despite substantial LTA remaining unutilised?
Our Analysis and Conclusions
13. We have heard the Learned Counsel for the Appellant and the Learned
Counsel for the Respondents at length. We have also carefully considered
Page 7 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
their respective submissions and the relevant material on record. Upon due
consideration of the arguments advanced and the documents placed before
us, we now proceed to analyse the issues arising for our consideration in the
present Appeal.
Issue 1: Whether the respective assets validly achieved
COD under the 2014 Tariff Regulations?
Submissions of the Appellant -TANGEDCO
14. PGCIL declared the Date of Commercial Operation (“DOCO” or
“COD”) of the assets in Appeal Nos. 329 and 56 of 2018 as 23.10.2016 and
13.11.2016, respectively. The CERC approved these DOCO based on the
RLDC certificate and the CEA clearance certificate.
15. TANGEDCO submitted that these technical certificates alone do not
satisfy Regulation 4(3)(ii) read with Regulations 12(1) and 12(2) of the 2014
Tariff Regulations in view of the facts of the case. The contention is that in
accordance with Regulations, DOCO could not have been declared without
beneficial use of the asset.
16. Reliance is placed on Appeal No. 123 of 2011 for the proposition that
a transmission asset can attain commercial operation only when it is put to
its intended beneficial use. Since one generating project did not get
commissioned, the other only had LTA to the extent of 558 MW, no external
beneficiaries were identified and the planned connectivity was incomplete,
the concerned assets could not be regarded as operational for their intended
purpose.
17. TANGEDCO also relied upon the order dated 15.09.2025 in Appeal
Nos. 206 and 332 of 2017, to contend that a DIC (Designated ISTS
Customer) cannot be saddled with charges for an asset from which it derives
Page 8 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
no corresponding benefit, especially where the asset cannot be utilised as
intended. An artificial DOCO, it submitted, cannot be used to impose PoC
liability upon DISCOMs.
18. It sought a declaration that DOCO was not validly achieved for want of
intended beneficial use, with transmission-charge liability for untied LTA
remaining upon the defaulting generators rather than existing DICs.
Submissions of the Respondent No. 2 - PGCIL
19. Respondent No. 2 submitted that the assets were completed in
accordance with the applicable Tariff Regulations and that TANGEDCO’s
admitted drawal of 558 MW from Coastal Energen through the system
established actual use from commissioning. The approval of COD is
therefore justified.
20. Respondent No. 2 contended that the RLDC charging certificate and
CEA clearance were only corroborative material establishing regular service;
they were neither the exclusive nor determinative basis of PGCIL’s
declaration.
21. Respondent No. 2 further relied upon proviso (ii) to Regulation 4(3),
which permits the transmission licensee to approach CERC for approval of
COD where regular service is prevented for reasons not attributable to it,
including delay in the concerned generating station or upstream/
downstream system. It submitted that Ind-Barath’s non-commissioning and
abandonment, along with the right-of-way delays set out in the tariff petition,
fall within that proviso. Thus, COD from 23.10.2016, as placed before and
accepted by CERC, is stated to conform to Regulation 4(3).
Page 9 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
22. Lastly, Respondent no. 2 distinguished Appeal No. 123 of 2011
pointing out that in that case the transmission line was not ready for use,
whereas the present assets were completed, commissioned and used by
TANGEDCO for drawal from Coastal Energen.
Submissions of the Respondent No. 20 - CTUIL
23. The transmission assets were, entrusted to PGCIL pursuant to CERC’s
regulatory approval, in proceedings where TANGEDCO’s predecessor,
TNEB, and other beneficiaries were parties. The approval was never
challenged and has attained finality.
24. CTUIL approached the CERC vide Petition No. 233/2009 concerning
the requirement for nine High Capacity Power Transmission Corridors,
including the Corridor in issue. CERC had granted regulatory approval for
the assets covered in the aforesaid petition vide Order dated 31.05.2010
noting that both IPPs had executed BPTAs, furnished Bank Guarantees and
completed the requisite milestones for grant of LTA, except for the MoEF
clearance in the case of Ind-Barath. In view of this it has been contended
that submission of TANGEDCO that CTUIL or PGCIL proceeded without
regard to the status of the generation projects or in disregard of the
applicable regulatory requirements is unfounded.
25. It has been contended that CTUIL had, from the outset, sought a
stronger performance-security mechanism, submitting that the then bank
guarantee of about ₹10-15 lakh/MW or ₹5 lakh/MW was inadequate to
protect developers and beneficiaries in implementing the identified high-
capacity transmission corridors. However, CERC did not issue such a
direction.
Page 10 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
26. CERC correctly declared COD under the 2014 Tariff Regulations.
Inclusion of a commissioned ISTS asset in the PoC pool is only a
consequential incident of COD under the Sharing Regulations, 2010 (Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of inter-State Transmission
Charges and Losses) Regulations, 2010). TANGEDCO has not shown how
COD contravened any applicable law.
27. Reliance on PSPCL v. PGCIL, Appeal No. 123 of 2011, decided on
02.07.2012, is misplaced, as that judgment did not interpret the 2014 Tariff
Regulations governing COD in the present case.
28. Even assuming any lapse by CTUIL in monitoring, it cannot deprive the
transmission developer of tariff after commissioning, particularly where the
system was developed under a final regulatory approval. In any event, CTUIL
continuously monitored the projects through Joint Coordination Committee
(“JCC”) meetings.
29. The JCC record relied upon by CTUIL shows:
• On 21.01.2015, Coastal Energen’s Unit 1 had achieved COD in December
2014; Unit 2 was expected by August-September 2015; its dedicated line
and bays were expected by March 2016; and its Unit 1 PPA with
TANGEDCO had been signed, while Unit 2 remained untied.
• By June/October 2015, Coastal Energen’s Unit 1 was commissioned and
Unit 2 was expected by November-December 2015. Ind-Barath’s Unit 1
was projected for March/June 2017, while Unit 2 had not been awarded.
• In February 2016, Coastal Energen was recorded as not attending, with
both units shown commissioned; Ind-Barath’s Unit 1 was projected for June
2018 and Unit 2 was abandoned.
• In June and September 2016, Coastal Energen’s two units were recorded
as commissioned. Ind-Barath acknowledged that it would be liable for
Page 11 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
transmission charges upon completion of the associated corridor; CTUIL
advised it to regularise the reduction in LTA. In September 2016, Ind-Barath
stated that 35% of its project had been completed, with ₹900 crore invested
out of ₹3,500 crore, but its project was uncertain due to non-signing of PPAs
and absence of tenders.
• By March 2018, Coastal Energen had relinquished 542 MW LTA pursuant
to CERC’s directions in IA No. 1/2018 in Petition No. 246/MP/2016, while
Ind-Barath informed that its generation project had been abandoned. By
December 2018, Ind-Barath’s DIC status had ceased and its LTA was
revoked.
Our Analysis and Conclusion on Issue 1
30. TANGEDCO has challenged date of commercial operation (DOCO) to
be 23.10.2016 for assets covered in Appeal No. 329 of 2018 and 13.11.2016
for assets covered in Appeal No. 56 of 2018 respectively, as approved by
CERC. The thrust of the contention is that in accordance with Regulations,
DOCO could not have been declared without beneficial use of the asset. In
this context, judgment dated 02.07.2012 of this Tribunal in Appeal No 123 of
2011 has been relied upon.
31. Before we proceed to analyse the issue, it will be worthwhile to peruse
the relevant Regulation of Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms
and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2014, which is extracted below:
“4. Date of Commercial Operation
The date of commercial operation of a generating station or unit or
block thereof or a transmission system or element thereof shall be
determined as under:
(1)…….
(2) ……..
(3) Date of commercial operation in relation to a transmission
system shall mean the date declared by the transmission licensee
Page 12 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
from 0000 hour of which an element of the transmission system is in
regular service after successful trial operation for transmitting
electricity and communication signal from sending end to receiving
end:
Provided that:
(i) where the transmission line or substation is dedicated for
evacuation of power from a particular generating station, the
generating company and transmission licensee shall endeavour to
commission the generating station and the transmission system
simultaneously as far as practicable and shall ensure the same
through appropriate Implementation Agreement in accordance with
Regulation 12(2) of these Regulations :
(ii) in case a transmission system or an element thereof is
prevented from regular service for reasons not attributable to the
transmission licensee or its supplier or its contractors but is on
account of the delay in commissioning of the concerned generating
station or in commissioning of the upstream or downstream
transmission system, the transmission licensee shall approach the
Commission through an appropriate application for approval of the
date of commercial operation of such transmission system or an
element thereof.”
32. We note from the Impugned Order that the argument about non-
beneficial utilization of the asset was put forward by TANGEDCO before
CERC as well. However, CERC had approved the DOCO based on the
certificate from RLDC and energization certificate from CEA. The certificate
from CMD, as mandated by the Regulations was not submitted by PGCIL in
case of assets covered in Petition No. 71/TT/2017 but the same was not
insisted upon by CERC with the direction that such certificate may be
submitted at the true up stage.
33. On the issue of DOCO, PGCIL has submitted that the asset has been
used by TANGEDCO for drawing 558 MW from Coastal Energen since its’
commissioning. This appears to be the factual position on perusal of the
submissions of TANGEDCO on the next issue i.e. sharing of transmission
charges.
Page 13 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
34. It is clear from the earlier extracted part of Regulation 4 of CERC Tariff
Regulations, 2014 that essential condition for declaration of DOCO is that
the asset should have been put in regular use. The term regular use has to
be differentiated from full use, which TANGEDCO seems to be insisting
upon.
35. It must be appreciated that transmission line is a lumpy asset and it
does not have a modular feature which enables its capacity to be
progressively augmented in small increments as system utilisation
increases. To take a simple example, suppose that, based on long-term
planning requirements, a transmission corridor is required to facilitate
transfer of up to 2500 MW of power from point A to point B. At the initial stage,
the actual power flow may, however, be only 150 MW. It would be fallacious
to contend that the transmission line should have been constructed only at
220 kV on the ground that such voltage level was sufficient to transfer the
initial 150 MW. It would be impractical to construct a 220 kV line initially,
decommission or replace it within a few years, and thereafter construct a 400
kV and ultimately a 765 kV line as the power flow progressively increases
towards 2500 MW. Such an approach would result in avoidable duplication
of investment, besides causing considerable difficulties in obtaining the
necessary Right of Way (ROW) and other statutory clearances.
36. This aspect assumes even greater significance in the present
circumstances, where obtaining ROW for transmission lines is becoming
increasingly difficult. Transmission planning, therefore, necessarily takes into
account the anticipated requirements over a reasonably long-term horizon.
A transmission line may accordingly be constructed at a higher voltage level
with higher capacity than what may be warranted merely by the power flow
prevailing at the time of its commissioning, so that the same transmission
Page 14 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
corridor can serve the system requirements over a much longer period. The
fact that the line is initially lightly loaded, therefore, cannot by itself lead to
the conclusion that the asset was not required or that it was not put to
beneficial use.
37. The possibility of modular augmentation is available, to some extent,
in the case of substation transformers. For instance, a substation may initially
be commissioned with a minimum configuration of two transformers to
provide the necessary operational reliability and redundancy, with additional
units installed progressively as system demand and power flows scale up. In
fact, investment in substation components can be strategically deferred by
temporarily operating a high-capacity transmission line at a lower voltage
level, as is the case here, where 765 kV transmission lines were initially
operated at 400 kV to match early-stage system requirements. Such
incremental or phased optimization, however, is generally not possible for
the transmission line itself.
38. It is also important to appreciate that a transmission line is not intended
to be operated continuously at its full thermal capacity. The permissible
loading of a transmission element is determined not merely by its thermal
rating but also by the requirement to maintain system security under credible
contingencies. In particular, the N-1 reliability criterion requires that with the
outage of any one element of a transmission corridor having parallel paths,
the system parameters, including voltage, loading and frequency, remain
within the permissible limits. Consequently, a transmission line may be
required to operate below its thermal capacity so that, in the event of an
outage, the power can be redistributed through alternate transmission paths
without resulting in unacceptable overloading and further tripping of
transmission elements. Such cascading outages can lead to widespread
disturbances and loss of load and/ or generation. Thus, low loading of a
Page 15 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
transmission line cannot, by itself, be regarded as evidence of under-
utilisation or non-utilisation of the asset.
39. More fundamentally, it is necessary to distinguish between utilisation
of the transmission capacity and availability of the transmission asset for the
intended purpose. A transmission asset is created not merely to carry a
particular quantum of electricity at the time of its commissioning, but to
provide the required transmission capability to the system. Its utility may
consist in providing transfer capability, reliability, redundancy, contingency
support and the ability to accommodate the anticipated growth in generation
and demand. The fact that the entire available capacity is not actually utilised
at a particular point in time does not mean that the transmission asset has
not been put to use or that the asset is incapable of performing its intended
function.
40. Indeed, the very purpose of transmission planning is to create the
required network in advance of the point at which the full capacity may
actually be required. If DOCO were to be recognised only when the
transmission asset is utilised to, or approaches, its full capacity, it would
effectively require the transmission system to be constructed only after the
requirement has already materialised. Such an approach would be
inconsistent with the very nature of transmission planning, which necessarily
involves anticipation of future demand and generation and provision of
adequate capacity in advance, including margins required for reliability and
system security.
41. Accordingly, the actual power flow on a transmission line at or
immediately after its commissioning cannot be the sole or determinative
criterion for deciding whether the asset has been commissioned and put to
use. Once the transmission asset has been completed, commissioned and
Page 16 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
is capable of performing its intended function as part of the transmission
network, the absence of full utilisation of its capacity cannot, by itself, justify
postponing its DOCO. To hold otherwise would equate the commissioning
and availability of a transmission asset with its instantaneous level of
utilisation, which is neither consistent with the manner in which transmission
systems are planned and operated nor reflective of the reliability and system-
security functions performed by such assets.
42. In the judgment dated 02.07.2012 in Appeal No. 123 of 2011, the Barh-
Balia line had merely been idle-charged from one end; the switchgear,
protection and metering arrangements at the other end were not ready and
no evidence of successful trial operation was produced. The Tribunal,
therefore, held that the line was not even ready for regular service and could
not attain COD merely because the components within PGCIL’s own scope
had been completed. In the present case, however, the Central Commission
recorded that the respective assets had been completed and were in regular
service, supported by the RLDC and CEA certificates; further, TANGEDCO
was drawing 558 MW of power from Coastal Energen through the
transmission system, which formed part of the meshed network. The
judgment in Appeal No. 123 of 2011 is therefore not applicable in the present
case.
43. We are constrained to observe that in spite of express provision in the
Regulations that the CMD’s certificate was mandatory and noting that the
same had not been furnished, the CERC vide Impugned Order dated
21.11.2017 in Petition No. 71/TT/2017 proceeded to approve COD as
23.10.2016 and relegated submission of the certificate to the stage of truing-
up that too without recording any reasons for such a course. The Central
Commission ought, to have insisted upon the certificate before approving
COD or recorded cogent reasons for permitting any departure from the
Page 17 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
requirement. Including a specific provision in the Regulations while framing
them, and thereafter ignoring the same provision at the stage of tariff
determination, without any explanation, is not expected of a regulatory
Commission. However, in the absence of any specific mention, we presume
that such certificate was submitted during the true-up proceedings. In view
of this, at this stage, we are not inclined to give much weightage to this issue.
We, however, advise the CERC to bear in mind that the applicable
Regulations, having the force of law, are required to be complied with not
only by those to whom they apply, but also bind the Commission and govern
the exercise of jurisdiction by this Tribunal, to the extent applicable.
44. In view of the foregoing analysis, we are of the opinion that the
contention of TANGEDCO that commercial operation of the assets could not
have been declared in the absence of their being put to what it terms as
“beneficial use” is devoid of merit. Accordingly, we conclude that CERC had
not erred in declaring commercial operation of the transmission assets
covered in the present Appeals.
Issue 2: Whether the subject transmission assets could be
included in the PoC mechanism and their charges recovered
from DICs, despite substantial LTA remaining unutilised?
Submissions of the Appellant- TANGEDCO
45. The scheme, according to TANGEDCO, was premised upon the
generators securing firm beneficiaries. At the Special SRPC meeting of
25.11.2010, PGCIL stated that the IPPs would bear transmission charges
until beneficiaries were firmed up. Clause 22.7 of the Detailed Procedure
required at least 50% of the LTA to be backed by PPAs three years before
Page 18 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
LTA operationalisation; upon failure, CTUIL was required to reconsider
implementation and where necessary, obtain CERC approval.
46. TANGEDCO submitted that only 558 MW was ultimately firmed up
through its PPA with Coastal Energen. Ind-Barath neither commissioned its
project nor had any PPA; Coastal Energen sought relinquishment of
substantial LTA. Thus, 1,442 MW of the 2,000 MW LTA remained unused and
without a procurer.
47. It is contended that the basis for the scheme had disappeared; the
IPPs’ dedicated evacuation lines and complete upstream/ downstream
connectivity were not established as envisaged; there was no 765 kV

Our Analysis and Conclusion on Issue 2
“Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.”
— Dwight D. Eisenhower, President of the United States (1953-1961)
70. We note that the core contention of TANGEDCO revolves around faulty
planning and its implementation. It is stated that the assets remain under-
utilized; the DICs should not be saddled with PoC charges corresponding to
this unutilized capacity; rather, such charges ought to be recovered from the
two generators who failed to achieve the generation capacity on which the
transmission network planning was originally premised.
Page 25 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
71. Having concluded in the Issue No. 1 that there was no error in the
declaration of the commercial operation of the assets in question, in our
opinion, it follows that recovery of transmission charges in respect of these
assets had to commence from the respective DOCO. The only question that
remains for consideration is as to how these transmission charges are to be
apportioned.
72. As regards contention of TANGEDCO that the two generators
responsible for under-utilisation of transmission assets should be made to
pay for it, we note that the CTUIL has levied relinquishment charges on Ind-
Barath and Costal Energen in accordance with the provisions of the CERC
(Grant of Connectivity, Long-term Access and Medium-term Open Access in
inter-State Transmission and related matters) Regulations, 2009. In this
context, it would be useful to refer to Regulation 18 of the aforesaid
Regulations, which is extracted below:
“18. Relinquishment of access rights.
(1) A long-term customer may relinquish the long-term access rights
fully or partly before the expiry of the full term of long-term access,
by making payment of compensation for stranded capacity as
follows: -
(a) Long-term customer who has availed access rights for at
least 12 years
(i) Notice of one (1) year – If such a customer submits an application
to the Central Transmission Utility at least 1 (one) year prior to the
date from which such customer desires to relinquish the access
rights, there shall be no charges.
(ii) Notice of less than one (1) year - If such a customer submits an
application to the Central Transmission Utility at any time lesser than
a period of 1 (one) year prior to the date from which such customer
desires to relinquish the access rights, such customer shall pay an
amount equal to 66% of the estimated transmission charges (net
present value) for the stranded transmission capacity for the period
falling short of a notice period of one (1) year.

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
(b) Long-term customer who has not availed access rights for
at least 12 (twelve) years - such customer shall pay an amount
equal to 66% of the estimated transmission charges (net present
value) for the stranded transmission capacity for the period falling
short of 12 (twelve) years of access rights:
Provided that such a customer shall submit an application to the
Central Transmission Utility at least 1 (one) year prior to the date
from which such customer desires to relinquish the access rights;
Provided further that in case a customer submits an application for
relinquishment of long-term access rights at any time at a notice
period of less than one year, then such customer shall pay an
amount equal to 66% of the estimated transmission charges (net
present value) for the period falling short of a notice period of one (1)
year, in addition to 66% of the estimated transmission charges (net
present value) for the stranded transmission capacity for the period
falling short of 12 (twelve) years of access rights.
(2) The discount rate that shall be applicable for computing the net
present value as referred to in sub-clause (a) and (b) of clause (1)
above shall be the discount rate to be used for bid evaluation in the
Commission's Notification issued from time to time in accordance
with the Guidelines for Determination of Tariff by Bidding Process for
Procurement of Power by Distribution Licensees issued by the
Ministry of Power.
(3) The compensation paid by the long-term customer for the
stranded transmission capacity shall be used for reducing
transmission charges payable by other long-term customers and
medium-term customers in the year in which such compensation
payment is due in the ratio of transmission charges payable for that
year by such long-term customers and medium-term customers.”
73. A careful perusal of the aforesaid provision makes it clear that the
compensation payable by an LTA customer upon relinquishment of its access
rights is linked to the transmission capacity that becomes stranded as a
consequence of such relinquishment. The compensation is determined with
reference to the estimated transmission charges attributable to such
stranded capacity for the period prescribed under Regulation 18, subject to
the specific conditions applicable to the nature and timing of the
relinquishment. Thus, the regulatory mechanism seeks to ensure that the
Page 27 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
financial consequences of stranded transmission capacity arising from
relinquishment are not left to be borne entirely by the remaining customers.
74. Significantly, Regulation 18(3) provides that the compensation so paid
by the long-term customer for the stranded transmission capacity shall be
utilised for reducing the transmission charges payable by other long-term
customers and medium-term customers in the year in which such
compensation payment becomes due, in the ratio of the transmission
charges payable by such customers. The Regulations, therefore, specifically
provide a mechanism for mitigating the burden of transmission charges on
other customers arising from stranded capacity.
75. We are conscious that the issue is presently the subject matter of a
separate litigation due to appeals filed by several generators who were
required to pay compensation for relinquishment of LTA in other transmission
schemes arising as a consequence of the order passed by the CERC in
Petition No. 92/MP/2015. Subject to the outcome of the said litigation, to the
extent any relief becomes available on account of the relinquishment
charges recovered from the concerned LTA customers, the DICs presently
bearing the transmission charges through the sharing mechanism would
correspondingly get compensated in respect of any unutilised capacity
covered by such charges.
76. It can thus be seen that, insofar as the sharing of transmission charges
is concerned, the CTUIL has followed the mechanism prescribed under the
applicable Regulations, including the mechanism specifically provided for
dealing with the financial consequences of relinquishment of LTA and the
resultant stranded transmission capacity.
Page 28 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
77. Another contention of TANGEDCO is that the Transmission Scheme
was undertaken by disregarding Clause 22.7(ii) of the detailed procedure,
which requires Generators to show PPA for at least 50% of their capacity.
78. We do not find merit in aforesaid contention since in its response, it
has been pointed by PGCIL that Clause 22.7(iv) of the same procedure
permits the Transmission Scheme to be undertaken with the approval of
CERC even where Generators failed to meet stipulated condition. It is
beyond doubt that the regulatory approval for the Scheme was granted by
CERC vide Order dated 31.05.2010 in Petition No. 233 of 2009.
79. TANGEDCO has also submitted that the basis for the scheme had
disappeared due to non-commissioning of Ind-Barath and only part capacity
materialising in case of the Costal Energen.
80. We have noted from the minutes of the Joint Coordination Committee
(JCC) meetings that first unit of Coastal Energen was commissioned in
December 2014. Further, in the 12th JCC meeting held in May 2015, Ind-
Barath had indicated expected commissioning of its first unit in March 2017.
In the next JCC meeting held in October 2015, this date was pushed further
to June 18. Ind-Barath first indicated abandonment of project in June 2016
and confirmed it in September 2016, while Costal Energen sought
relinquishment of part LTA capacity after the transmission assets had already
been commissioned.
81. In view of the aforesaid facts, we find considerable force in the
submission of PGCIL that by time Ind-Barath had informed abandonment of
its generation project, execution of the scheme had progressed to such an
extent that it could not had been altered.
Page 29 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
82. It is well recognised that planning, however carefully undertaken, is
necessarily based on assumptions and projections about future
developments, and there is always a possibility that actual developments
may differ from those envisaged at the time of planning. A good planner does
not remain passive when the assumptions underlying a plan do not
materialise; rather, the plan is suitably adapted to the changed
circumstances so as to ensure that the assets created continue to serve their
intended purpose and are utilised efficiently.
83. The same principle applies with greater significance to transmission
planning, given the large and lumpy nature of transmission investments. If,
for instance, a transmission line has remained substantially under-utilised
because the generation envisaged at the connected generating stations did
not materialise, the appropriate response should not necessarily be to regard
the line as an inefficient investment and leave it under-utilised. The planning
process should instead consider whether generation capacity can be
developed or facilitated at the concerned stations, or whether other suitable
generation or demand can be connected, so that the available transmission
capacity is put to effective use.
84. We note from the minutes of the joint study meeting of Southern
Region held on 10th and 11th May 2018 which were submitted by TANGEDCO
as part of their rejoinder dated 13.11.2018 that though Coastal Energen has
LTA of 558 MW, but entire capacity (2 x 660 MW) is being pooled at Tuticorin
Pooling station. Further, generation from Kudamkulam NPP (2x 1000 MW)
and Tuticorin JV (2 x 500 MW), which were not specifically mentioned in
planned scheme, is also being pooled at Tuticorin Pooling station. Thus,
utilization of the assets in question is not limited only for transfer of 558 MW
to Tamil Nadu.
Page 30 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
85. As a broad analogy, the situation may be compared with the
development of an apartment complex by a group housing society. Suppose
an architect designs the complex, including common facilities such as a park,
clubhouse and other amenities, based on the number of flats proposed and
the anticipated occupancy. If fewer flats are subsequently occupied, the
architect cannot, merely for that reason, be held responsible for the under-
utilisation of those facilities, provided the design was appropriate on the
basis of the information, projections and assumptions reasonably available
at the time of planning.
86. The same principle would apply to a contractor who constructs the
complex in accordance with the approved design. The contractor cannot
ordinarily be faulted merely because some facilities are subsequently under-
utilised. The position may be different if, before the relevant stage of
execution, the contractor was instructed to defer, modify or omit any facility;
though such a change may also have cost and contractual implications.
Further, if the contractor is also responsible for maintaining the common
facilities and is entitled to recover the admissible fixed costs, lower
occupancy would not, by itself, justify a reduction in such recovery. The cost
is incurred for creating, operating and maintaining the facility and keeping it
available. It does not necessarily depend upon the extent to which the facility
is actually used at a particular time.
87. A similar principle applies to transmission planning. The planning
agencies may broadly be compared with the architect. Their role is to assess
anticipated system requirements, apply the prescribed planning criteria and
design the transmission network accordingly. The transmission licensee
may, in turn, be broadly compared with the contractor. Its role is to implement
the approved transmission scheme in accordance with the directions of the
competent authority. The transmission licensee is also responsible for
Page 31 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
operating and maintaining the transmission assets under the provisions of
the Act. Under the applicable tariff and transmission-charge sharing
framework, it is entitled to recover its admissible annual fixed costs. Such
recovery cannot, by itself, depend upon the actual utilisation or power flow
through an individual transmission element at a particular point in time. The
relevant consideration is whether the capacity has been created,
commissioned, maintained and kept available in accordance with the
applicable regulatory requirements.
88. Thus, if a transmission asset was planned and implemented on the
basis of the requirements, information and assumptions reasonably
prevailing at the relevant time, its subsequent under-utilisation would not, by
itself, establish an error in planning or implementation. Nor would lower
utilisation, by itself, justify denial or reduction of otherwise admissible fixed-
cost recovery.
89. The relevant questions would be whether there was a reasonable basis
for the capacity and configuration approved; whether the licensee
implemented the approved scheme as directed; whether the asset has been
maintained at the prescribed level of availability; and whether any
subsequent change required the competent authority to defer, modify, stage,
abandon or otherwise alter the scheme.
90. The PoC mechanism also proceeds on this broad principle. The costs
of the inter-State transmission system are pooled and shared among the
designated ISTS users in accordance with the applicable framework. Once
a transmission asset is completed, commissioned and made available as
part of the approved transmission system, its admissible costs form part of
the common transmission-cost pool. The rationale underlying this approach
appears to be captured, albeit briefly , in the CERC’s description of the basis
Page 32 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
for sharing the transmission charges among all DICs, namely, that the
transmission system forms part of a meshed network.
91. The fact that an individual asset may, at a particular time, be used by
fewer users or carry lower power flows than anticipated does not make the
cost of the created capacity disappear. Subject to the applicable regulations,
tariff orders and any valid direction regarding deferment, modification, non-
commissioning or abandonment, the transmission licensee remains entitled
to recover its admissible annual fixed costs.
92. This approach is also consistent with the nature of transmission
planning. Transmission systems are planned not only for present flows, but
also for anticipated demand and generation, reliability, contingency
requirements, security of supply, evacuation needs, redundancy and future
system requirements. Such planning necessarily involves uncertainty
regarding the timing of demand, generation addition and changes in system
conditions. Therefore, subsequent lower utilisation cannot, without more, be
treated as conclusive evidence of imprudent planning or as a basis for
denying recovery of otherwise admissible fixed costs.
93. In view of the foregoing, it is evident that in the present case, the
foundational assumptions on the basis of which the transmission scheme
was planned did not fully materialise. However, the non-materialisation of
these assumptions cannot, by itself, be attributed to any lapse, imprudence
or deficiency on the part of PGCIL, which implemented the scheme in
accordance with the approved transmission plan and the investment
approval. Accordingly, PGCIL is entitled to recovery of the transmission
charges in respect of the subject assets through the PoC mechanism, in
accordance with the CERC Sharing Regulations, 2010, subject to the
Page 33 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
Commission’s prudence check and determination of the admissible capital
cost.
94. We have also considered TANGEDCO’s submission that the impugned
orders are non-speaking. The requirement that a quasi-judicial authority
must record reasons is indisputable; however, the adequacy of reasons must
be assessed with reference to the issue decided and the material
considered. In the present case, the CERC has given a reason for including
the transmission charges in the PoC mechanism for sharing by all DICs,
namely, that the assets form part of the meshed transmission network. The
reasoning is brief, but it cannot, therefore, be said that the Impugned Orders
are wholly without reasons. At the same time, the fact that the assets form
part of a meshed network does not, by itself, necessarily preclude bilateral
billing. There have been instances where bilateral billing has been imposed,
particularly in cases of default. This aspect seems to have been missed by
the CERC. The reasoning, therefore, does not adequately explain why, in the
facts and circumstances of the present case, the transmission charges were
required to be shared through the PoC mechanism by all DICs.
95. Thus, while the Impugned Orders cannot be characterised as non-
speaking, they do fall short in adequately explaining the rationale for the
conclusion reached. We recognise that a reasoned order should ordinarily
set out adequate justification for the conclusions arrived at. However, the
absence of more elaborate reasoning, by itself, cannot be a ground for
setting aside the Impugned Orders, particularly when the entire record, the
applicable Regulations and the submissions of the parties are before us. The
issues have also been fully argued before this Tribunal. We have, therefore,
considered and determined the substantive challenge on its merits, as set
out above.
Page 34 of 35

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of 2018
ORDER
For the foregoing reasons as stated above, the Appeal Nos. 56 and 329 of
2018 are dismissed. Accordingly, the Impugned Orders dated 19.09.2017 in
Petition No. 235/TT/2016 and dated 21.11.2017 in Petition No. 71/TT/2017
are upheld.
The Captioned Appeal and pending IAs, if any, are disposed of in the above
terms.

clarification of judgment dated 07.08.2025 passed by this Tribunal vide
which the appeal no.109/2022 was disposed of.
2. The order dated 30.09.2020 passed by the Uttar Pradesh Electricity
Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”) in
petition no.1365/2018 was under challenge in the above noted appeal.
Vide the said impugned order, the Commission had rejected the claim of
the appellant for acknowledging certain events pleaded therein as Change
in Law (CIL) events in terms of Article 10 of the Power Purchase
Agreement (PPA) dated 15.03.2016 executed between the
appellant/applicant and the respondent nos.1-4. However, the
Commission had acknowledged the increase in Electricity Duty on
Auxiliary Consumption as Change in Law event and had allowed its
impact to the appellant along with carrying cost.
3. In the judgment dated 07.08.2025 this Tribunal acknowledged (i) the
increase in GST on O&M charges pursuant to notification dated 28.06.2017
issued by the Ministry of Power, and (ii) increase in transportation cost on
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.1270/2026 in Appeal No.109/2022 Page 3 of 9

account of 100% fly ash disposal requirement as stipulated by notification dated
25.01.2016 issued by Ministry of Environment and Forests, as Change in Law
events and remanded the matter back to the Commission for computation of
impact of these Change in Law events upon the appellant. It needs to be noted
that two more Change in Law claims had been made by the appellant in the
appeal which were rejected in the said judgment.
4. The contention of the appellant/applicant is that while directing the
Commission to compute compensation for the two Change in Law events as
acknowledged by this Tribunal in the judgment dated 07.08.2025, this Tribunal
did not make any observations on the aspect of carrying cost/interest to which
the appellant is entitled with effect from the dates when these two Change in
Law events had occurred, despite the appellant having specifically made a
prayer for carrying cost in the prayer clause of the appeal and also having urged
the same during the course of hearing of the appeal.
5. Learned senior counsel for the appellant Shri Sajan Poovayya submitted
that absence of any express observation qua carrying cost in the said judgment
is being construed by the respondents as rejection of the prayer regarding
carrying cost, and therefore, necessity arose for filing the instant application
seeking clarification on this aspect.
6. We find it relevant to note here that the appellant had assailed the said
judgment dated 07.08.2025 of this Tribunal before the Hon'ble Supreme Court
by way of Civil Appeal No.57880/2025 qua the Change in Law claims which
were disallowed by this Tribunal in the said judgment. The Civil appeal has

been dismissed as withdrawn by the Hon'ble Supreme Court vide order dated
08.12.2025 while granting liberty to the appellant to avail such remedies as may
be available to them as per the directions of this Tribunal. The said order dated
08.12.2025 passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court is extracted hereinbelow: -
“1. Mr. Sajan Poovayya, learned senior counsel
appearing for the petitioner seeks permission to withdraw
the appeal.
2. Permission, as sought for, is granted.
3. The Civil Appeal is, accordingly, dismissed as

such remedies as may be available to them as per the

(Emphasis supplied)
7. Mr. Nalin Kohli, learned senior counsel appearing on behalf of the
respondents has vehemently resisted the application. He would submit that in
the Civil Appeal filed by the appellant before the Hon'ble Supreme Court,
rejection of the prayer for carrying cost/interest on the acknowledged Change
in Law claims was also raked up and since the Hon'ble Supreme Court was
inclined to dismiss the appeal at the threshold, the appellant withdrew the
appeal and therefore, the claim for carrying cost/interest now agitated by the
appellant in the instant application is in the teeth of limited liberty granted by the
Hon'ble Supreme Court. He would further argue that instead of pointing out any
ambiguity, clerical slip, accidental omission etc. in the judgment dated
07.08.2025 of this Tribunal or difficulty in its implementation, the appellant is
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.1270/2026 in Appeal No.109/2022 Page 5 of 9

seeking to agitate a new substantive relief which cannot be granted in the garb
of application for clarification. It is also argued by the learned counsel that even
otherwise also this Tribunal has become functus officio and thus, precluded
from entertaining the instant application of the appellant.
8. What is material to note here is that in the judgment dated 07.08.2025,
this Tribunal, while allowing the two Change in Law claims of the appellant, has
not considered or discussed the prayer of the appellant for carrying cost on the
financial impact of Change in Law claims. The judgment is totally silent on this
aspect.
9. We may note that as per the settled legal principle, the purpose and
object of allowing a relief to a claimant for the Change in Law event is to restore
affected party to the same economic position as if the Change in Law had not
occurred. It cannot be gainsaid that when a Change in Law event occurs, the
affected party starts incurring additional costs from the date of the said event,
and therefore, if only the principal compensation i.e. the increased cost on
account of Change in Law event is allowed to the affected party without carrying
cost, the affected party cannot be said to have been restored to its original
economic position. This would defeat the very purpose of having a Change in
Law clause in the PPA.
10. The legal principle emanating from the various judgments of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court namely Uttar Haryana Bijli Bitran Nigam Ltd. v. Adani Power
Ltd. (2019) 5 SCC 325, Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.1270/2026 in Appeal No.109/2022 Page 6 of 9

Commission etc. is that a Change in Law clause in a PPA is an inbuilt
restitutionary principle which compensates party affected by such Change in
Law and which must restore, through monthly tariff payments, the affected party
to the same economic position as if such Change in Law had not occurred. The
Commission or this Tribunal shall have due regard to this principle while
determining the consequences of Change in Law event.
11. In the instant case, Article 10.2 of the PPA specifies the application and
principles for computing impact of Change in Law and the same is extracted
hereinbelow: -
“10.2 Application and Principles for computing
impact of Change in Law
10.2.1 While determining the consequence of Change in
Law under this Article 10, the Parties shall have due
regard to the principle that the purpose of compensating
the Party affected by such Change in Law, is to restore
t/1 rough monthly Tariff Payment, to the extent
contemplated in this Article 10, the affected Party to the
same economic position as if such Change in Law
has not occurred”
(Emphasis supplied)
12. It is, thus, evident that the Change in Law clause of the PPA also is in line
with the legal principles enunciated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the above
noted judgments entitling the affected party to be restored, through monthly
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.1270/2026 in Appeal No.109/2022 Page 7 of 9

tariff payments, to the same economic position as if such Change in Law had
not occurred.
13. Having said so, we are of the opinion that the judgment dated 07.08.2025
passed by this Tribunal in appeal no.109/2022 suffers from an ambiguity or an
accidental omission on the aspect of carrying cost as the same has neither been
noted nor discussed anywhere in the judgment. The impact of the Change in
Law events allowed to the appellant in the said judgment would evidently be
incomplete, in case, the carrying cost also is not granted on such impact of the
Change in Law events to the appellant. In fact, carrying cost is the
compensation for time value of money, and therefore, any compensation for a
Change in Law event is totally inadequate if the same does not come with
carrying cost. The object of carrying cost is to offset the impact of deferred
recovery of legitimate expenses incurred by the affected party on account of
incurring additional costs due to the impact of Change in Law event. Therefore,
in case, carrying cost is not allowed to the appellant herein on the Change in
Law claims which have been acknowledged by this Tribunal in the judgment
dated 07.08.2025, the appellant would not be restored to the original economic
position and thus, would defeat the entire purpose of the Change in Law clause
contained in the PPA.
14. The argument advanced by Mr. Nalin Kohli, learned senior counsel that
this Tribunal, after passing the judgment dated 07.08.2025, has become functus
officio and therefore, cannot entertain this application, is without any force. It is
_________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.1270/2026 in Appeal No.109/2022 Page 8 of 9

a trite law that every court or tribunal is empowered to clarify or rectify any
ambiguity or inadvertent omissions in the order/judgment passed by it either on
its own motion or on application submitted in this regard by any of the parties.
Further, the order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No.57880/2025
also does not put any embargo upon this Tribunal to entertain the instant
application. The Apex Court has manifestly granted liberty to the appellant to
avail the remedies as may be available to them as per the directions of this
Tribunal. This indicates that the Apex Court has left it for this Tribunal to issue
any directions as would be deemed fit and necessary in the fact and
circumstances of the case.
15. Hence, in the light of the above discussion, we hereby allow the
application and clarify that the Commission shall compute the impact of the two
Change in Law claims, acknowledged by this Tribunal in the judgment dated
07.08.2025, upon the appellant along with carrying cost applicable under the
relevant regulations.
